title: Certified measurement and control of an entanglement-breaking index on programmable hardware
abstract: The entanglement-breaking index of a quantum channel, the number of self-compositions after which the channel destroys all entanglement with any reference, has to our knowledge never been measured. We show that a certified thermal collision feedback loop makes this integer both measurable and controllable on current programmable hardware, every load-bearing quantity delivered as an interval-arithmetic certificate. On the measurement side: a target list for the integer staircase n_EB(p) with decision-point negativities certified at margins 0.025 to 0.109; an exact per-round depolarising model in which the selected staircase survives realistic noise as certified integers; an exact, tight compilation of the round unitary (seven CNOTs all-to-all, five native arbitrary-angle gates, ten on heavy-hex); and a 33-million-draw gated search bounding the thermal valley's contrast by a wall with an interior maximum, a certified 2.85x10^-3 near floor 89. On the control side: the model composes rounds of differing bath polarisation exactly, so the valley becomes a pulsed valve, switching at a certified minimal pulse of exactly eight rounds; the optimal pulsed signal, a certified 3.43x10^-3, beats the static protocol, so the best valley measurement is intrinsically pulsed; and a coherent tilt of the bath Bloch vector lifts the signal to a certified 8.6x10^-3, three times the static ceiling, at zero population cost. Valley signatures certifiably die near per-round noise strength 10^-4, fixing the error-extrapolation burden. The staircase is a near-term experiment; the pulsed valley a precisely priced one.
summary: This work provides a highly rigorous framework for measuring and controlling the entanglement-breaking index of a quantum channel on programmable hardware. By employing advanced interval arithmetic certificates, the authors prove that this index is measurable via a 'staircase' protocol and controllable using optimized pulsed operations. This advances the field by moving beyond mere simulation to certified, hardware-implementable quantum characterization.
main_problem: The paper addresses the measurement and control of the entanglement-breaking index, $n_{EB}(\Phi)$, of a quantum channel, a quantity previously unmeasured.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that $n_{EB}(\Phi)$ can be both rigorously measured and actively controlled on current programmable hardware using certified feedback loops and pulsed operations.
method: The methodology relies on advanced 'certification discipline' using ball arithmetic at 256 bits to provide rigorous, mathematically guaranteed bounds on physical observables.
model_or_system: The system models a quantum channel $\Phi$ acting on a message qubit, which interacts with fresh two-qubit thermal ancillas via a 'collision feedback loop.' The channel evolution is parameterized by bath polarization $p$.
key_observables: The entanglement-breaking index $n_{EB}(\Phi)$ (an integer), negativity, and the contrast of the 'thermal valley' are key observables.
important_parameters: The analysis involves noise strengths ($\lambda$), bath polarizations ($p$), and specific pulse lengths (e.g., minimal pulse of exactly eight rounds).
main_assumptions: The rigorous claims are based on the use of ball arithmetic and certified mathematical proofs; non-certified results (like the 33-million-draw search) are noted as such.
figures_summary: The notes refer to a 'pulse atlas' detailing minimal switching pulse requirements and tables comparing signals achieved via coherent tilts versus static thermal protocols.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework for the index, details the measurement program (staircase), and then develops the control mechanism, showing that pulsed operations outperform static ones, culminating in a comparison between thermal and coherent control.
why_interesting: The rigorous, certificate-based approach to characterizing channel properties like entanglement breaking is highly relevant to quantum information theory, providing new tools for benchmarking quantum hardware.
